newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan hostage envoy looks forward to sushi.
newsitem.headline: Japan hostage envoy looks forward to sushi.

text.p: Japan's "samurai" ambassador Morihisa Aoki arrived home on Monday after the Lima hostage siege, hungry for sushi, eel and a bowl of noodles.
Aoki's return to Tokyo in a wheelchair coincided with new rumblings between Japan and Peru about whether force was needed to end the four-month-long standoff.

There was only a low-key welcome for the silver-haired Aoki, who was applauded for his stoic bravery during the crisis but faces close questioning about security lapses that led to Marxist rebels taking over his home.
Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels took over Aoki's residence on December 17 during a lavish reception celebrating the birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito.

The event turned into a nightmare, with the rebels first holding hundreds of guests and then gradually releasing most of them, until there were just 72 hostages left in the residence when it was stormed by the Peruvian military last Tuesday.

"Now that I'm back in Japan I'm desperate to enjoy sushi, soba (Japanese noodles) and eel," said Aoki, who with his wife Naoko accompanied Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda on the 18-hour chartered flight from Lima.
Aoki, 58, who injured his legs and hips when he jumped from the second floor of the building, said he wanted to go back to work as soon as possible and to return to Peru.
But he was careful not to link the two wishes, saying his desire to return to Peru was to thank the Peruvian people for their support during his ordeal.
"People of my generation are workaholics. If we take a long rest, we feel irritated. I want to go back to work as soon as possible," he told journalists at Tokyo's Haneda international airport.
A Foreign Ministry official said there was no chance of Aoki returning to work until he passed extensive medical checks.
"He looks OK now because he is on a high. But he needs microscopic medical checkups," the official told Reuters.
From the airport, Aoki went straight to hospital along with two diplomats who were also hostages throughout the siege.
All but one hostage was rescued alive in last week's raid, which freed all 24 Japanese captives. One Peruvian hostage and two soldiers died along with all 14 MRTA rebels.
Aoki would not say if he believed lax security led to the crisis.
"I will make it clear after sorting it out myself and reporting to Prime Minister (Ryutaro) Hashimoto," he said.
In Lima on Saturday, Foreign Minister Ikeda said Peru had primary responsibility for security at Aoki's home.

Japanese media reported on Monday that in an interview Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori hit back at criticism that he did not consult Tokyo in advance of the raid and that negotiations, not force, could have ended the siege.
"Japan believed the residence was like an impenetrable fortress. We thought the Japanese government would reject our plan as not plausible if we consulted them in advance," he said.
In the reports, carried by all major Japanese newspapers, Fujimori sidestepped accusations that some of the rebels who took over the embassy were executed in the rescue mission.
"The order was to save the 72 hostages... Anything could happen under those circumstances, in the midst of a battle," Fujimori said.
"If anyone in Japan defends the Tupac Amaru, please let me know. We have 2,000 dangerous Tupac members in Peruvian prisons and we can export them," Fujimori said.
